name: Ivan Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play organ for a small chapel, cover two local choirs and record hymn practice lines for their singers. I earned a music degree and have worked at the keyboard for twenty-eight years. I like when a whole room finds the same beat; I do not like being told a rehearsal is 'voluntary' after the call was made.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How steady is that work at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, my partner sells produce at a market stall, and our children are grown. We rent and have about ten days of expenses saved. My pay is low for an experienced organist and few similar posts are near the bus line. I use a paper service book and have never used AI.

say: I'd accept **faster notices** with paid service and rehearsal fees on the page.
I'd remind the chapel the **organ needs hands** at the keys.
think: A **cancelled wedding** could leave rent short even without major AI.
Our **ten-day reserve** and variable stall takings offer little cover.
do: Request **six paid services**, written cancellation rate and two choir calls tomorrow.
Keep **paper service book** and save twenty from an extra cleared wedding after rent, food and travel.
feel: I feel **anxious** about ordinary paid-service gaps.
S0.quote: A quicker notice cannot make a cancelled wedding pay.
fieldNote: His **low experienced pay** and ten-day reserve make a moved ceremony immediately material to rent.
He **never uses AI** and keeps a paper service book for signed calls.

steps.text: Request six paid chapel services, cancellation rate and two choir calls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the chapel that faster printed notices are fine if the paid service and rehearsal fees are on the page. The organ still needs a pair of hands at the keys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even if AI barely matters, a cancelled wedding service can leave rent short. Ten days saved and the market stall's changing takings are a narrow bridge between payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll ask the chapel secretary for the next six paid services and a written cancellation rate, and keep my two choir calls. In the first year of this mild picture I'll continue with my paper service book and save twenty from an extra cleared wedding fee only after rent, food and organ travel are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about our ordinary gaps in pay. A quicker notice cannot make a cancelled wedding pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when a ceremony moved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A couple moved their ceremony after I had arranged a replacement at the market stall. The secretary paid nothing because we had no written cancellation clause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try an AI calendar?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I do not use an AI calendar. I can read the chapel's signed book and mark my own pages.

say: I'd ask whether software will replace **paid hymn recordings**.
I'd demand **written fees** for playing and preparation before contract changes.
think: Hymn lines bring **one-quarter of my pay** and may lose buyers.
Our **ten-day reserve** cannot cover a long committee delay.
do: List **twelve hymn invoices** and request a signed minimum paid rehearsal schedule.
Keep **organ and choir calls** while asking the guild to review recording rates before signing.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my own hymn-fee income shrinking.
S1.quote: A guild can read a contract, but it cannot make a chapel book a rehearsal.
fieldNote: He seeks **contract help** through a musicians guild while retaining existing paid organ and choir work.
He **declines new AI use** unless paid demonstration, commercial permission, storage and singer consent are established.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the chapel committee whether software will replace the paid hymn practice recordings. I would ask the committee for a written fee covering my playing and preparation before it changes the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those hymn lines bring about a quarter of my own pay, and buyers may stop ordering them. Ten days saved does not let me wait for a committee to remember the lost fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll list the last twelve hymn invoices and ask the chapel for a signed minimum paid rehearsal schedule. In the first year of change I'll keep organ services and both choirs, and ask the local musicians guild to review any recording-rate cut before I sign it; I will not put singers' voices in a new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic loss of hymn fees. A guild can read a contract, but it cannot make a chapel book a rehearsal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the chapel's new recording tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I won't use the chapel's recording tool without a paid demonstration, a paid-use licence, approved storage and written singer consent. I would still check every note against the score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the guild check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want the guild to mark the preparation hours and cancellation rate in the contract. I will bring invoices rather than ask it to guess my pay.

I'd ask for **signed live services** while the chapel hires players.
think: I expect **one-quarter pay** from hymn recordings to end in 2028.

do: Count **hymn invoices**, request signed chapel calls and an actual pension estimate before stopping work.
Seek **posted accompanist work** after live cuts only if degree/experience qualify, written net after travel replaces lost fees and bus hours fit.
Keep **chapel and choirs** until a suitable signed offer arrives.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about expected pay loss against ten days saved.
S2.quote: I cannot put an old accompanist advert in the rent book.
fieldNote: Expected **2028 recording loss** precedes 2031 organ-playing robots.
A real job needs **posted eligibility**, written replacement net pay after travel, workable bus hours and signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the chapel that thinking AGI by 2028 could make hymn practice lines cheaply. Organ-playing robots follow around 2031; I would ask for signed live services while people still hire a player.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect those recording orders to end in 2028 and take a quarter of my pay. The paid chapel services may hold, but ten days saved cannot carry even that first loss for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll count recording invoices, ask for signed paid chapel calls and request an actual pension estimate before discussing any stop at 60. In the first year after 2028, if organ services also fall, I'll seek a posted paid arts-centre accompanist job only if my music degree and choir experience meet its rules, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the bus reaches its hours; I'll keep the chapel and choirs until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about the expected quarter of my pay disappearing with only ten days saved. I can look for a real vacancy, but I cannot put an old accompanist advert in the rent book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is an accompanist job open now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There is no arts-centre offer on my table. A job must be posted with paid hours and requirements before I count it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you know about retirement income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not seen our pension statements. I will ask for the actual figures; a birthday will not pay our flat rent.

I'd demand **rehearsal wages** in the contract before 2034 robots.
think: I will not risk **rent savings** on an unbooked room class.
do: Request **two-year paid schedule** with written minimum fees, preparation hours and cancellation pay next month.

Seek **posted community work** only if live services also fall, degree/experience qualify, written net after travel replaces loss and bus fits.
feel: I feel **anxious** about recording loss, with live calls still possible.
S3.quote: I will not describe unsigned rehearsal hours as wages to my partner.
fieldNote: His **traditional approach** is a paid written service contract, not an unfunded class.
The **job search** requires additional live cuts, posted eligibility, written after-travel replacement net and signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the chapel council that five years to AGI by 2031 gives us time to write a paid organ-service agreement, not a promise in a hallway. Playing robots come around 2034; the first issue is whether rehearsal wages are in the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hymn recordings could end before 2031 under ordinary software. I would rather secure live services than hire a room and hope strangers buy lessons when our rent reserve is ten days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I'll propose a two-year paid chapel service and rehearsal schedule with written minimum fees, preparation hours and cancellation pay. In the first year after 2031, if recording orders stop, I'll keep only booked paid organ and choir calls and ask the guild to enforce the written minimum; if the chapel cuts paid services too, I'll seek a posted community music job only if my degree and choir experience qualify, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and bus hours fit, keeping current work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing recordings, but a signed live schedule would give us some ground. If both recording and service fees go, our reserve will not hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the council refuses the schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The council can refuse a two-year schedule. I will not describe unsigned rehearsal hours as wages to my partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the guild help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guild can compare each paid call with the signed schedule and ask for a missed fee. I still need the chapel to book actual services.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown children that ten years to AGI by 2036 gives us time to get pension figures and paid chapel calls on paper. Organ-playing robots follow around 2039, but rent comes every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may still need paid organ services. Ten days saved today and an unknown pension are no reason to put a retirement date on the calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request actual pension statements and signed paid chapel calls. I'll save ten percent of each extra cleared wedding service fee after rent, food and travel toward one month of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I'll keep paid chapel and choir dates while booked, and if live services fall and the pension figures leave a gap, I'll seek a posted paid part-time music role only if my degree and experience qualify, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and bus times fit; I will stay until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a long run of low pay even with more warning. A pension statement will tell us more than a friend's guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra wedding pays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there is no extra paid wedding, there is nothing to save from it. I won't shift food money to pretend the target is met.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop playing at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will not stop at 68 simply because a form calls me old. I will check the real pension amount against rent and actual paid calls.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because hymn recording fees could stop before the chapel agrees to more paid services. Signed chapel calls, real pension figures and a posted qualifying job with written after-travel pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a player travels to a service when the fee is late. The organ will be ready on Sunday, but the bus still needs cash on Saturday.

headlineQuote: The organ will be ready on Sunday, but the bus still needs cash on Saturday.
portrait: Ivan is a **58-year-old experienced organist** with a music degree, partner and grown children.
His **low pay**, ten-day reserve and few nearby jobs make late service fees a rent problem.
He **never uses AI** and seeks written minimum fees and cancellation terms through chapel and guild.
He requests **actual pension figures** and keeps paid music until a suitable signed replacement offer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove a quarter of Ivan's income from hymn recordings.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed chapel calls**, actual pension figures and posted qualifying work with written after-travel replacement pay would help.
